meningioma.name: Meningioma
meningioma.what_it_is: A tumour that grows from the meninges, the protective layers surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Most are non-cancerous and slow-growing, and many cause no symptoms until they become larger.
typical_next_steps: See a GP, who may carry out simple checks of eyesight, balance and memory
The GP may refer you to a neurologist or neurosurgeon for further tests
Management depends on the tumour's type, location and symptoms, and may involve monitoring rather than immediate treatment
self_care: Keep a written record of symptoms with dates, which helps the specialist assess any pattern or change
Pace yourself and get enough rest; fatigue is common
You must tell the DVLA (or your local licensing authority) if you are diagnosed with a brain tumour that needs treatment
If you have had a seizure, stop driving and inform the licensing authority
After a seizure, take showers rather than baths and take extra care with cooking, fires and gardening
Alcohol in moderation is generally fine, but it can trigger seizures in people who have them
meningioma.source: NHS Benign brain tumour (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/benign-brain-tumour/); Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Living with and beyond a brain tumour (https://www.leedsth.nhs.uk/services/brain-tumour/living-with-and-beyond-brain-tumour/)

glioma.name: Glioma
glioma.what_it_is: A tumour originating from the glial cells that support the brain. Gliomas can be non-cancerous or cancerous, and are graded by how quickly they grow.
typical_next_steps: See a GP about any persistent symptoms
A specialist referral is usually needed to determine the tumour's type and grade
Further tests after an initial scan establish the grade and the appropriate treatment
self_care: Keep a written record of symptoms with dates, so changes over time are visible to your specialist
Pace yourself and allow time to rest
You must tell the DVLA (or your local licensing authority) about the diagnosis, and you must not drive while a brain tumour is suspected
If you have seizures, stop driving, take showers rather than baths, and take care around cooking, fires and gardening
Tell your doctor if seizures begin or become more frequent
glioma.source: NHS Brain tumour (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/brain-tumour/); United Lincolnshire Hospitals NHS Trust, Seizures and brain tumours (https://website.ulh.nhs.uk/documents/patient_information_leaflets/)

pituitary.name: Pituitary tumour (adenoma)
pituitary.what_it_is: A growth in the pituitary gland, a small gland at the base of the brain that produces hormones. Most are non-cancerous. Some produce hormones; others cause symptoms by pressing on nearby structures such as the optic nerves.
common_symptoms: symptoms related to hormone changes such as fatigue
typical_next_steps: See a GP about vision changes or persistent headaches
Referral usually involves both a neurosurgeon and an endocrinologist (hormone specialist)
Pituitary function tests, including hormone levels, are typically carried out
self_care: Note any changes in vision, energy levels or mood, with dates, to discuss at your appointment
Take any prescribed hormone medication exactly as directed, since pituitary tumours can affect hormone balance
Pace yourself and rest when tired
Tell the DVLA (or your local licensing authority) if the tumour affects your vision or needs surgical treatment
pituitary.source: NHS Benign brain tumour (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/benign-brain-tumour/); Cambridge University Hospitals, DVLA driving regulations for brain tumours (https://www.cuh.nhs.uk/patient-information/dvla-driving-regulations-brain-tumours/)

no_tumor.name: No tumour detected
no_tumor.what_it_is: This scan did not show features the system associates with the tumour types it was trained on.
typical_next_steps: A result of 'no tumour detected' does not rule out a tumour or any other condition
This system examines one slice from a scan, not a full study, and was trained on only three tumour types
If you have symptoms such as persistent headaches, seizures, vision changes or weakness, see a GP regardless of this result
self_care: If you have ongoing symptoms, keep a diary noting what they are, when they occur and how long they last
Seek an urgent GP appointment or call your local urgent-care line if a headache is severe, sudden, or comes with vomiting or confusion
Do not treat this result as a reason to delay seeing a doctor about symptoms that concern you
